en: In the ninety-first section of the *Zhongbian* (Selection from the Middle) compiled by Shi Dunlun,
there are three verses at the beginning that collectively list four gates. There are already three verses that explain what precedes them.
There are three gates.
Now, there is one verse that explains the fourth gate, the gate of detachment from desire and so forth;
within this, there are further seven gates.
First, those who are free from desire and those not yet free from desire;
second, the inquiry;
third, the causal conditions; fourth, the paths of defilement.
Five: protecting life.
Six: the characters "fixed abode" (*sthāna*) and so forth.
Seventh: in the initial explanation within the prose commentary, the distinction between those who have abandoned desire and those who have not is clarified.
Regarding the statement "if there is a bhikṣu... even unto ultimate nirvāṇa":

whether he has already become free from desire for this realm of desire, he remains defiled by the three types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) throughout the three times within the stages of meditative concentration.
If one has not yet abandoned desire, then regarding the phenomena cognized by the mind among the five types of sublime sensual pleasures,
one is likewise defiled throughout the three periods of time by the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the three latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
One does not abide in, nor enter into, ultimate nirvāṇa.

In this context, "the consciousness that grasps based on the past" refers to the arising of various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) from the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses of the past.
Regarding the statement that "the future world belongs to that appropriating consciousness":

it should be understood that the clinging consciousness of the present belongs to the future world, which consists of the entanglements (paryavasthāna) associated with that [appropriating consciousness] along with its auxiliary companions.
Because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) constantly follow and pursue the continuum, those who maintain that they grasp the appropriating consciousness (ādāna-vijñāna) are incorrect;
the latent dispositions cannot take that consciousness as an object.
It is merely designated as such a consciousness by virtue of the sense of being bound.
The second question and answer.
Although the answer contains four points of intent, it clarifies the fourth [point]: the Buddha as the Great Teacher.
There are two reasons for questioning:
one is to inquire deliberately despite already knowing the answer;
the third explains the underlying causes and conditions.
One interpretation holds that the six internal bases serve as the cause because they are that upon which the seeds depend;
although "internal" refers to the six bases, the term "mind" here specifically takes up the sixth base, the mental faculty (*manas*).
There is the ālayavijñāna which maintains the seeds;
this is one interpretation.
According to the principle of "concomitant transformation," this applies even to the five material sense-faculties, which likewise receive and assimilate habitual tendencies.
Why is it that regarding the various seeds, one does not say that the external six bases (āyatana) maintain the seeds, but explains only the internal six bases?
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:
"Furthermore, the internal six bases constitute a continuous and homogeneous series."
Because that which was previously attained continues until the end of life and is ultimately transformed;
objects of perception are not like this, as they lack the former two meanings.
This is the fourth explanation of the path of defilement.
What are called the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are the pathways of defiled conduct.
Since desire and greed serve as the roots of defilement,
they are termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Fifth, the explanation of preserving one's life.
Regarding the two locations:
first, preserving one's own life when it might suddenly be cut short by untimely death.
The two unwholesome minds lead one to perish and go to the various evil destinies.
What is meant by "relying upon appropriate mental attention" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*)?
Furthermore, from which two kinds of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) should one liberate the mind?
Thus, there are two questions.
The answer to the first clarifies "attention according to reality" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
which can be understood from the text as it stands.
Answer: There are two types of defilement: first, when one is walking and so forth;
second, when one dwells in seclusion and so forth.
It should be understood that within this context, "reaching a similar fruit" refers to these states.
The second defilement arises from the first defilement;
therefore, they are called cause and effect.
However, this is not a primary causal relationship.
Therefore, it is said they are "similar.
The sixth [section] explains the locus of attachment;
the seventh explains the word "equal" (sama).
There are two further aspects of the apprehended object;
these can be understood according to the text.
Above, within the analysis of the bases (*āyatana*), there is one and a half verses that serve as a summary verse.
The first half-verse summary contains four sections;
the latter single verse summary also contains four sections,
with each line constituting one section.
Thus, from among the four subsequent individual verses, one gate is extracted from each and incorporated into this general verse.
Within the first individual verse, there are nine gates;
the first is the "homogeneity of cause" (*hetu-sabhāgatā*).
Second, volition;
third, bondage and liberation;
fourth, characteristics.
Fifth, the universal contact;
sixth, resolute confidence;
seventh, guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
The eight teachings;
the nine aspects of affection;
and within the prose commentary, first the explanation of the commonality of causes.
Master Jing said:
"The 'consciousness of the homogeneous class' (sabhāga-vijñāna) still possesses a portion.
It is said that the noble disciples enter into non-self by means of this consciousness of the homogeneous class as one gateway."
Abiding in the correct contemplation of all consciousnesses by means of three characteristics constitutes the second gateway.
Next, the first gateway will be explained in sequence.
Regarding the phrase "by manifesting the five visible material bases":
These are the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). That which is the body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is the five sense faculties (*pañca-indriya*).
As for "increasing" or "decreasing": [it refers to their respective variations].
The arising of the five sense objects is called "increase";
their ceasing and passing away is called "decrease.
As for "taking" or "discarding":
When consciousness arises in the five sense faculties, the grasping of objects is called "appropriation" (*upādāna*);
when there is no consciousness, it is called "relinquishment" (*ujjhanā*).
Because they are impermanent by nature, those consciousnesses that engage with their respective objects follow into impermanence and so forth.
The sense faculties and their objects are impermanent;
the consciousness produced from them is likewise so.
Because they are impermanent, they are suffering.
Because it is suffering, there is no self;
this is the first gateway taught.
How does one, having entered into the nature of selflessness, proceed until reaching and abiding in right contemplation?
This is the summary.
Below, the three characteristics are explained:
first, since the view of self is the root of all false views, it must necessarily be severed first.
Second, one contemplates that consciousness follows the distinctions of each sense organ and object, being immeasurable.
Third, one contemplates that this consciousness does not abide for even a single moment, let alone eternally.
Master Da says:
Regarding "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*):
because the faculties and their objects possess functional capacity and are able to give rise to consciousness.
Because the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) apprehend the same object, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Question: If that is so, why are the five material bases (*rūpāyatana*) also called "homogeneous"?
Answer: Because they are homogeneous with respect to what is produced by the faculties and consciousnesses, they are termed "homogeneous by cause" (*hetu-sabhāga*).
Regarding the statements "whether increasing or decreasing," "whether grasping or relinquishing," each is explained comprehensively:
the five sensory objects and the five sense faculties are predominant.
Therefore it is said, "if increasing";
or at times there is decrease,
therefore it is said, "if decreasing."
Because the faculties and their objects increase, there is grasping;
because the faculties and their objects decrease, there is relinquishing.
Therefore it is said: "whether grasping or relinquishing."
Furthermore, another interpretation is that if there is an increase or decrease, it refers specifically to the attachment to the five external sense objects; therefore,
it says "if there is an increase."
Because external objects are subtle and inferior,
it is said that they "diminish.
As for those who engage in grasping or rejecting:
This refers specifically to the internal faculties;
because external objects increase, they are grasped,
and because external objects decrease, they are relinquished.
The second explanation concerns reflection.
The statement "regarding the reduction of the six sense bases, up to 'one should not reflect,' etc.
clarifies that the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the six sense bases is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
One should not engage in conceptualization, discrimination, or interrogation;
rather, one should rely solely on the wisdom of awakening to investigate and so forth.
What are these four?
That is to say, there may be existence or non-existence, or difference or non-difference.

By way of contrast, the arising and ceasing of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) possess four modes of activity (*ākāra*) which clarify the four modes of activity of the aforementioned unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because those six sense bases have arising, they are termed "existence."
That which has ceased is called "non-existence.
It is distinct in dependence upon others;
it is non-distinct because there is no difference between its preceding and succeeding moments within its own continuum.
From "the six sense bases having been eternally extinguished" onwards,
it is illogical to observe the four aspects of the unconditioned in accordance with their formal definition.
The following clarifies that frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) refers to speech that induces the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*);
if one diligently engages in such frivolous proliferation regarding its objects,
it only causes harm and provides no benefit.
The third is liberation through the unraveling of bonds.
In the verse, the meaning of "liberation" (vimukti) applies both to the higher and lower vehicles;
here, however, it refers specifically to liberation from bondage.
In the lower section, it says, "the characteristic of liberation.
This is the fourth characteristic of liberation.
Master Jing said:
One who has well-cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and severed the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) remains unchanged in body and mind even when their person is harmed or their life is taken.

By virtue of well-guarding the sense faculties, they attain liberation from the four types of suffering and obtain four kinds of joy: first, the joy of being liberated from the suffering arising from external conditions in the future.
Second, one attains liberation from suffering through internal dependent origination in the future;
third, at the time of parinirvāṇa in the present life, one attains liberation from all sufferings of both external and internal bases;
fourth, after the end of life, one is similar to grass and trees.
There are two kinds:
first, the six sense bases are like grass and trees that lack a self;
second, the six sense bases are like grass and trees burned by the fire of the three poisons.
That the noble disciples’ non-arising of future suffering resembles a small portion of the Buddha’s power of clarity refers to liberation and so forth;
it is not because suffering does not arise due to conditions in the present life.
Unlike [ordinary beings], for the Tathāgatas, all conditions for suffering in the present life do not arise;
even if suffering should momentarily arise in a Buddha, it is swiftly severed.
Furthermore, the two kinds of power of clear knowledge (*vidyā-bala*) of all Tathāgatas are entirely perfected and equal.
The two types of clear knowledge—of cessation and of non-arising—are both fully accomplished.
Master Tai said:
"After the death of one who has no further training (aśaikṣa), suffering does not continue, being similar to grass and trees."
Once dead, it does not continue further.
Master Da said:
"It is due to two kinds of supports."
First, the basis of affliction;
second, the basis of retribution.
Regarding the two kinds of power of clarity:
The untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) is called "clarity" (*vidyā*);
furthermore, because it possesses the power of being untainted, it is also called "power" (*bala*).
This is the fifth explanation regarding the pervasiveness of contact (*sparśa*).
Master Jing said:
"It is said that there is a śramaṇa who transcends superior direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); even worldly fools are not deluded by him, let alone those with wisdom.
He is like the five consciousnesses, which clearly manifest the five sense objects."
If even fools practice [these views], how much more so those who possess wisdom?
Nevertheless, the various non-Buddhists engage in false speculations;
some rely on the past limit (*pūrvānta*) to give rise to four types of erroneous doctrines.
Alternatively, four false doctrines are established based on the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
This opens two gates;
below, these two gates will be explained in sequence.

The general meaning clarifies that various non-Buddhists fail to understand that all suffering and pleasure arise from contact (*sparśa*), and thus falsely speculate that they are created by self, another, or both.
Here, the correct principle is clarified: feeling (*vedanā*) arises only through the conjunction of the three.
Therefore it is said: "In this context, only the arising of suffering and pleasure through the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses can be apprehended.
This passage is explained as proving that [suffering] is not produced by past actions, based on the evidence of superior direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Even worldly fools would not be so deluded;
yet those śramaṇas and others, contrary to direct perception (pratyakṣa), posit such things as past actions (pūrvakṛta).
Therefore, it is said that they "transgress superior direct perception."
The sixth [section] concerns superior resolve (*adhimukti*).
Within it, the first part clarifies how the outflows (*āsrava*) are swiftly exhausted by means of four aspects;
the second part provides a detailed explanation.
This refers to the three trainings and five types of persons.
Within this, first the names of the six bases and the three trainings are listed;
subsequently, the practice of the five types of *pudgalas* based on the six kinds of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) in reliance upon the three trainings is presented.
First, the ordinary person living at home is bound only to sense objects and seeks liberation from them.
Second, although the ordinary person who has already gone forth possesses a resolute conviction in practicing non-afflictive conduct through the three types of action based on ethical discipline.
The third is the resolve of detachment from the desires of the desire realm belonging to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The fourth is the resolve of the exhaustion of craving belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*).

The fifth consists of two resolves belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): the resolve based on the exhaustion of the fifth appropriation (*upādāna*) and the resolve of non-forgetfulness of the sixth mind.
It should be understood that the first and second types of resolute conviction serve as the basis for the training in ethics;
the third type of resolute conviction serves as the basis for the training in the mind;
and the final three types of resolute conviction serve as the basis for the training in wisdom.

If one understands that it is by means of this wisdom that afflictions are abandoned, and that the abandonment of afflictions is called "non-forgetfulness," this is the resolution of the sixth [topic].
Furthermore, the exhaustion of the cause for future existence is called the "exhaustion of craving."
The fourth [point] is explained:
that which is called the "exhaustion of grasping" refers to the severance of the defilements of manifest objects.
The fifth [point] is explained.
Furthermore, that first person, up to and including those who undergo transformation, is not yet capable of relinquishing the bondage of objects;
the second is unable to abandon the practice of affliction or the practice of transformative affliction; and the third is unable to relinquish desire or transformative desire.
Alternatively, the fifth person among the five explained below provides the seventh explanation:
guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
The eighth explains the teaching on liberation;
the ninth explains the characteristics of craving.
Both can be understood by following the text.
Next, there are two verses containing twelve sections:
first, the object-condition alone;
second, thorough investigation.
Third, the vow;
fourth, the restraint of all aspects;
fifth, non-restraint upon entering the holy teaching.
Sixth, being well-prepared with the six superior provisions;
seventh, abandoning what has been learned;
eighth, the point of attachment.
Nine: the meaning of the unwholesome;
ten: following the stream;
eleven: the Bodhisattva’s superiority over other vehicles.
In the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*,
within the prose section,
the first explains the "sole condition" (*ālambana-mātra*).
Master Jing said:
"Karma, afflictions, and their own seeds are the causal conditions that project the feeling;
the six bases of contact, in relation to feeling, serve solely as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) by way of being its support."
The following provides an analogy to clarify this:

Just as when the mind initiates an effort that draws forth various acts of grasping and receiving, the hand can only serve as an auxiliary condition for grasping and receiving—such as when one intends to grasp grass or wood.
The mind is the cause for grasping;
the hand is the condition that assists grasping.
Master Da said:
Now, the Mahāyāna Dharma is the primary cause for the arising and sustenance of life through the mind; therein,
the hand serves as an auxiliary condition that assists in its production.
It also performs its livelihood.
Herein, the karma produced by the mind is a metaphor for the causal conditions of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The mention of "the hand" is a metaphor for contact (*sparśa*) as the condition for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*);
thus, it refers to the present condition.
The second [section] explains the investigation of examination (*vitarka-paryeṣaṇā*), as in the text.
The third explains the vow (*praṇidhāna*).
Master Jing said:
"As for the statement 'if there are bhikṣus... even increasing further,' this refers to a bhikṣu who does not seek or desire future existence."
At most, one should undergo only seven existences.
Because of the seeking of further existence,
the causes of suffering increase manifold in the seventh existence, exceeding seven and reaching eight.
As long as one has not yet conceived the intention to flee, one perceives oneself as bound by bonds;
because this occurs at the very moment of bondage and liberation, it is described as "subtle.
It is not called subtle because the instruments of bondage, such as iron or wood, are difficult to discern.
After the arising [of the thought], it is difficult to discern the moment of the vow; both are subtle.
Master Da says:
"Whether they be devas or non-devas."
"Prisoners" refers to human beings.
"Those who are not gods" refers to ghosts,
spirits, and the like.
Regarding the statement, "If this arises, one is bound by what is attained and subject to prohibitions":
when the mind of flight and concealment is stirred, one is naturally bound;
it is not through another person that the binding is accomplished.
If one has not previously given rise to the intention to flee, one naturally dwells in peace and happiness, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses;
it is because of this temporal state that they are said to be "subtle.
Yet, at other times, because an evil mind arises, one is bound.
No one can bind it,
yet it is naturally bound;
therefore, it is called "subtle."
Fourth is the explanation of the restraint of all aspects (*sarvākāra-saṃvara*).
Within this, seven chapters are first opened,
which are subsequently explained in sequence.
"Restraint and non-restraint" can be understood according to the text.
Next, the soft, medium, and superior grades of mundane restraint will be explained.
Master Jing says:
Regarding the attainment of the four types of mental engagement within the superior mundane [attainment],
these seven mental engagements are subsumed into four.
This refers to the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of effortful application (*abhisamskāra*) and so forth.
This [attainment] consists of the mental orientations within the *anāgamya* concentration and the eight fundamental dhyānas.
As for the nine stages of mental abiding (*navākārā cittasthiti*):
That is to say, it causes one to abide in peace and happiness.
Furthermore, regarding the tenfold distinction based on the differences in the supports for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
this is the first section.
Due to temporal distinctions, there are many hundreds of variations.
This is the second section.
Regarding the tenfold distinctions of the first section:
First, the three categories beginning with "with vitarka" exhaustively include all factors of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Second, the three categories of "concomitant with the three feelings" also exhaustively include all stages.
Third, the four divisions beginning with "regression" exhaustively include all concentrations (*samādhi*).
They are distinguished by way of their gates;
there is no separate dharma apart from them.
One should know that, within this context, the first two types of restraint are to be analyzed.
Regarding those subsumed under the power [of application]: the two lower grades are included;
the latter one, subsumed under the power of cultivation, is the superior grade.
Master Da says:
Regarding "the mundane [levels] of inferior,
middling, and superior": because the faculties, the prātimokṣa vows, the dhyāna vows, the shared vows, and so forth, possess inferior, middling, and superior degrees,
and because they are *sāsrava* (with outflows), they are called "mundane."
In this context, the first two grades—the soft and the medium—are distinguished by means of the faculties and the prātimokṣa vows within the stages of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection.
The superior grade is distinguished by means of the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation; it is precisely the dhyāna restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara).
The passage beginning with "After they have already matured" clarifies the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
The passage beginning with "Having cultivated that" [clarifies the same].
This clarifies the untainted precepts of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Fifth is the explanation of "not being protected" according to the sacred teachings;
first, the general heading.
Next, the third section is explained separately.
Within this, the passage beginning with "What is meant by non-restraint" and following is a further detailed analysis.
Regarding the wisdom of hearing that accords with supernormal power (*ṛddhi*):
it is said that the illumination of the object by the wisdom of hearing is itself termed "supernormal power.
This constitutes the sixth stage, wherein the superior provisions for liberation are well-prepared.
Regarding the statement that "craving for joy serves as the basis for inducing old age and death in both the present life and future lives":
within the present life, one is driven toward old age and death by engaging in unchaste conduct through the influence of craving.
That which draws forth the old age and death of the present life, leading one toward the miserable destinies,
is called the "old age and death of future lives.
As for the phrase "like grass and trees," etc.:
The wisdom derived from hearing the True Dharma is like grass and trees;
practice in accordance with the Dharma is like a raft.
One initiates practice in accordance with the Dharma by means of the wisdom of the True Dharma.
Just as grass, wood, and so forth can be used to construct a raft;
this is the seventh [point], the relinquishing of what has been studied,
which occurs through seven causes and conditions.

The first refers to the five stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), namely the five stages concerning the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), as previously explained.
The second refers to "or again, [the stage] of ordinary beings and below"; it should be understood that the latter five causes and conditions also include the character "and" (*yǒu*).
The eighth explains the point of attachment,
as in the text.
The ninth explains the meaning of unwholesome.
Master Jing said:
"Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of gates that can produce sublime wisdom and the vision of non-perversion,
I shall now explain the meaning of 'one reception' (ekāgratā) as it evolves through these four gates."
Regarding the liberation through the four kinds of sublime knowledge,
as for the observation of suffering: first,
one understands that the five aggregates act as the cause capable of producing the three types of sensation.
Furthermore, it is explained that the three types of contact serve as the causes capable of producing the three types of sensation.
Moreover, regarding the internal six sense bases which act as the support,
and the external six sense bases which act as the causal basis for that support:
This is the gateway of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, regarding the cause for abiding,
the four nutriments (*āhāra*) serve as the cause for the abiding of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).
Furthermore, regarding those who practice in accordance with suffering, pleasure, and so forth, based on the nature of their own conditions and their accompanying factors,
there is the gateway of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
"Basis" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
The conditions refer to the six sense objects;
the intrinsic nature refers to the six consciousnesses;
and the associates refer to the various mental factors that arise simultaneously.
The feelings arising from contact associated with suffering and so forth depend upon the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, for two reasons, the Tathāgata eliminates the doubts held by those who are unskilled in the meaning:
first, that a single name expresses a single meaning through various phrases and syllables.
Second, the revelation of the extensive meaning of the holy teachings.
Below, while distinguishing the middle [meaning], the first gate is not explained; only the extensive meaning is distinguished.
That is to say, from the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*), one immediately understands the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
The second, the stage of skillful means, consists of the four roots of goodness;
the third, the stage of vision;
and the fourth, the stage of cultivation.
The five stages of one beyond training (*aśaikṣabhūmi*).

Among these, one who dwells having perfected the faculties of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-indriya*) is such that the fulfillment of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is termed the "ultimate limit."
Those who dwell in the maturation of the faculties, from those transformed by the Tathāgata up to those who have achieved right view,
are precisely those for whom the preceding fulfillment of the factors conducive to liberation has been transformed by the Buddha, such that they have achieved the wisdom born of hearing.
This is the stage of skillful means for the bodhisattva who relies upon this [practice] up to the simultaneous cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

Within the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), he first contemplates that consciousness and form are impure; because the craving-consciousness does not arise, this constitutes the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Immediately thereafter, those who are able to enter into clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Noble Truths possess the stage of clear vision (dṛṣṭi-bhūmi).
Furthermore, they cultivate the path as it has been attained, gradually progressing toward higher stages.
That which is the stage of cultivation is that by which one can attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows;
this is the stage of no-more-learning.
In the following example, because the remaining three stations of consciousness serve as the three foundations of mindfulness,
it is said that "as for the 'able,' so too is it for the 'reaching' (*yathābhūta*)."
Conditioned by consciousness, one dwells in feeling; this is the foundation of mindfulness of suffering.
Conditioned by consciousness, one dwells in perception; this is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind as impermanent.
The foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) consists of taking consciousness conditioned by formations as its object;
this is [the contemplation of] non-self.
Furthermore, one may contemplate all four foundations of mindfulness through the aspects of suffering, impermanence, and so forth.
The Master Da said:
"The bhikṣus herein do not understand that the Tathāgata should teach through various different gateways within a single meaning;
therefore, it is said that they are 'not skilled in the meaning.'"
Regarding the sublime knowledge that understands, as it truly is, the cause for the arising of feeling:
first, because of joy and pleasure, the five aggregates arise;
this joy is craving, and thus it is able to moisten and activate karma.
Because it can produce that which is categorized as "feeling" (*vedanā*) among the five aggregates, it is called the cause for the arising of feeling.
Furthermore, it is said: "With the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), there is the accumulation of feeling."
If one follows this principle,
contact is the cause for the arising of feeling;
this refers to immediate conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the external six sense-objects which serve as the support,
the internal five faculties are the causal basis upon which they depend.
The tenth [section] explains the following of the stream.
Regarding the statement "establishing the object of focus within the continuum":
this refers to how Māra and others, desiring to entice and delude sentient beings,
manifest various subtle and exquisite objects.
Eleventh, explaining how the Bodhisattva excels other vehicles.
First, a general introduction identifying and listing eight characteristics;
subsequently, an explanation of these in sequence.
Regarding the phrase "there are bodhisattvas who exist in the future":
these are those who practice the true path and will dwell in the tenth stage within the realm of Maheśvara, where they shall attain perfect enlightenment in the future.
Because it is difficult to understand, only the eightfold manifestation of the path in the nirmāṇakāya is taught.
Descending from Tuṣita to be born among humans is called the "Bodhisattva in his final existence.
As for those who correctly practice the path and its fruits, and so forth:
Jingyun: The "right path" is the fruit of wisdom.
As for the "fruit of the path," it refers to the fruit of cessation, meaning the severance of the two obstructions.
The fruit of abandonment thus attained is also superior to that of the śrāvakas and is unsurpassed.
There is another interpretation:
the "right path" refers to the noble path.
The fruit of the Path is Nirvana.
In the commentary, it says:
"The fire of the three poisons is like a cock perched upon both banks."
The Tripitaka Master said:
"Upon both banks of the river of birth and death, there are fire-cocks of the three poisons.
Whenever sentient beings raise their heads, they are immediately scorched."
Therefore, this metaphor of the rooster represents the three poisons.

It refers to non-Buddhists who, regarding seven locations, conceive of them as places where a self dwells.
One falls into the seven stations of consciousness and is born in the three lower miserable realms;
now, the noble disciple does not conceive of a self within the seven stations of consciousness,
nor does he continue the seven stations of consciousness in the miserable realms by taking birth in the lower states.

Furthermore, regarding the passage from "giving rise to that sphere of consciousness" up to "becoming an arhat," what is here called the "sphere of consciousness" refers to the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The two spheres refer to the realms of suffering and perception, which are the evil destinies (*apāya*).
Although Arhats manifestly undergo old age and death,
they are said to have attained dissociation from them; likewise,
although they manifestly experience [suffering] and possess name-and-form, [they are dissociated from them].
However, the name [of that realm] is obtained through dissociation from it.
Master Da further stated:
"Thereafter, those who are reborn below it continue in the sphere of infinite consciousness."
That which lies beneath the seven stations of consciousness refers to the three evil realms;
furthermore, it is within those that consciousness arises.
The fourth dhyāna and the heaven of the perception of compassion—
these two places are not abodes where consciousness delights to dwell.
As for those [beings] who abide in consciousness therein:
These are the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Regarding "and two locations," one interpretation states they are the three evil destinies (*durgati*).
In the second and fourth dhyānas, as well as in the Heaven of Non-perception,
there are sentient beings who are bound yet free from bondage during the stages of the path of preparation and the path of accumulation.
The noble disciples have already subdued the view of self;
therefore, they are said to be "detached" (visaṃyukta).
However, they have not yet abandoned the fetters of the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
Therefore, it is said that there are fetters.
Because within them, the presence or absence of fetters cannot be discerned,
it is said to be difficult to understand.
The Second Major Section:
Explaining the Two Truths and Other Topics.
First, the verses enumerate seven sections.
First, the fruit;
second, the conventional and the ultimate;
third, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
4. This-action and so forth;
5. The five great emptinesses;
6. Differentiation.
Seventh, "self-action.
In the prose commentary,
the first part explains the different categories (*paryāya*).
Because the ignorant and the wise differ,
it is called a "differentiation of gates.
As for the statement regarding the two kinds of root afflictions:
[These are] ignorance and craving.
Second, the explanation of the two truths:
first, it is generally explained that because the noble ones realize the two truths, they do not give rise to the grasping at a self.
Next, the skillfulness regarding the two truths is specifically distinguished.

As for the statement that "there is also no non-acting which does not possess the meaning of auspiciousness," this means that there is no non-acting of wholesome causes that does not result in the production of fruit.
Thirdly, regarding the passage beginning with "furthermore, with respect to consciousness, contact, sensation," and so forth—
which generally explains various phrases within the sūtra—
Master Jing’s commentary states: "Furthermore, one contemplates consciousness, contact, sensation, perception, volition, and the body as suffering."
The names and forms and the six sense bases are omitted for brevity.
Because of the accumulation of causes, suffering likewise accumulates and arises in accordance with how those causes have accumulated.
"Because the cause ceases, that which corresponds to its cessation—
suffering— also ceases.
This is because it is according to the extent of what exists and the manner in which it exists, following their respective order.
What was previously stated— that such mental attention is cultivated through the causes and conditions of mundane attention belonging to the meditative stages—
is done by way of exhausting all possibilities (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
Now, regarding the time of entering into the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths and so forth:
This is the nature of things as they are (yathāvadbhāva).

Furthermore, there is the wisdom of those in training (śaikṣa) called "the sublime wisdom of entering and emerging from the world," which emerges from birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and subsequently submerges back into it.
Master Tai said:

"The well-versed noble disciple who is skillful regarding all dependent origination understands, as they truly are, the principles of the two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—and this is designated by the distinct term 'knowledge'."
This refers to the first, "good vision," up to the tenth, "discriminating wisdom.
Regarding the third, [it is said to be] the understanding of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Master Jing’s commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "due to two causes and conditions, up to the point of all that undergoes transmigration":
it may be that the essence of dependent origination arises as a single substantial entity,
yet it arises in dependence upon conditions.
Therefore it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Because it arises by depending on conditions,
it is called "dependently arisen."
Furthermore, it is explained that the cause is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and the fruit is dependently arisen (pratītyasamutpanna).
That is to say, ignorance is dependent origination.
Regarding "conditioned arising" and so forth:
within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), two aspects are established.
These are: "in accordance with how [it] evolves" and "that which evolves," as explained below.
Explaining the two divisions:
herein, regarding the twelve links that flow in the sequence of cause and effect according to reason as appropriate,
one understands them as they thus flow.
Furthermore, this sequence of cause and effect that accords with reason,
established through successive transmission since beginningless time, is called the *dharmatā*. In the present it is called the abiding of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*),
and in the past it is called the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharma-niyama*).
It should be named "the suchness of phenomena" (*dharmatā-tathatā*), and so forth.
This explains all that undergoes cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Master Da explained it thus:
In this context, because the principle of dependent origination possesses the characteristic of the Buddha-nature as being eternally abiding,
it is said to be "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena).
Second, regarding the conditions:
First, that which undergoes the process of flowing forth is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Second, all things that flow forth are called dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Regarding the distinction between these two:
first, the productive cause is called dependent origination.
The second refers to the fruit produced, namely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Above, there has been a general explanation of dependent origination;
hereafter, the specific distinctions shall be explained.
Furthermore, from "this which accords with reason" onwards,
[the text] explains the specific names for the dharmas that arise naturally (*dharmatā*) within the sūtras.
Moreover, regarding these two kinds of skillfulness:
The first [interpretation] states that it refers to cause and effect;
the second states that it refers to skillfulness regarding the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional.
The fourth [interpretation] explains this as "performing" and so forth.
"First, because cause and effect are connected as one" explains that it is not the case that one acts and another experiences [the result].
"Because the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) differs between the prior and subsequent [moments]" [explains this further].
The explanation that [suffering] is not created by oneself and experienced [by another] is twofold: first, because the remaining agent and experiencer cannot be found;
second, because a master who performs the action and undergoes the experience cannot be found.
Fifth, the explanation of the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Master Jing and others state:
"As for 'the non-self of the *pudgala* up to its being unobtainable'..."
This means that apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising through dependent origination, there is no real self.
Regarding the statement "the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) extends to impermanence":
when one desires to enter this gateway, one understands that because formations (*saṃskāra*) are not-self, they are termed "selfless formations" (*anātmasaṃskāra*).
Previously, it was taught that there is no person apart from the aggregates;
this is called the practice of emptiness.
However, within the text, it speaks of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising from conditions do not exist as real entities; setting aside their conventional designations, this principle is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Furthermore, the subsequent emptiness refers to the selflessness of phenomena, while the preceding clarification that there is no person outside of these formations refers to the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
The subsequent explanation follows the text:

one should understand that the name "Tathatā" (Suchness) signifies the nature of reality as it is (*yathābhūtatā*), and that the name "Tathatā" signifies the nature of non-perversion (*aviparyāsatā*).
This refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The sixth [section] is the explanation of discernment.
One should know that all dependent origination is established by means of two causes and conditions.
This consists of a general heading followed by a detailed explanation.
Regarding "the nature of all that exists" (yathāvadbhāvatā) and "the nature of the full extent of existence" (yāvadbhāvatā):
these two gateways may be explained solely in terms of the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness),
or they may be explained solely in terms of practice (*caryā*).
Next, these two are explained.
Either principle (*yukti*) is "as-it-is" (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) and phenomena (*vastu*) are "as-far-as-they-go" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*);
however, in this present passage, they are distinguished solely with respect to phenomena.
The correspondence between cause and effect, such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*),
is called "as-it-is" (*yathāvadbhāva*).
Furthermore, all these various distinctions, such as ignorance being the condition for volitional formations, are fully encompassed within conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
This is called "exhausting all that exists.
Regarding the seventh [point], the interpretation of "acting for oneself," Master Jing said:
It is said that what is received is grasped by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for craving itself [to grasp], because craving is still a form of seeking;
it clarifies that feeling (*vedanā*) does not seek for itself.
The self-generated recipient of sensation is also that which the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) apprehends through another.
This is the interpretation of the Master Daśabala, based on the commentary on the Tripiṭaka.
Because of the accumulation of joy, there is the accumulation of feeling,
as previously stated. As previously stated, because all phenomena lack any real activity,
there is no self-agency that can appropriate another.
If one claims that there is no self, yet a divine self (īśvara) or another agent appropriates the experience of others,
it is not logical to say that another is the creator.
Because there is no such thing as a self (ātman).
Therefore, the Commentary says:
"It is also as previously stated."
As before, because there is no self (ātman),
there is no agent for future lives;
this refers to the extreme of the three types of evil causal theories mentioned previously.
First, self-creation;
second, creation by another;
third, both.
This is not reasonable;
therefore, it is called the "Treatise on Evil Causes. As for the latter type of non-causationist view, it establishes four propositions regarding arising without cause.
